---
title: "Fifty-two weeks of New York"
description: "A year of hourly temperatures as 52 stacked ridgelines, white on black, after Joy Division's Unknown Pleasures. Then the same poster cycling through New York's three airports."
categories: [Statistical, Effects, Animation]
image: figs/ridgeline-poster.png
---



The cover of Joy Division's *Unknown Pleasures* is a stack of 80 radio pulses
from a pulsar, each line drawn a little lower than the one before and hiding the
lines behind it. The same picture works for anything that has a distribution per
row. Here each row is one week of 2013 and the line is that week's spread of
hourly air temperatures in New York: narrow and cold at the top, broad and warm
in the middle, cold again at the bottom.

The data is `weather` from the [nycflights13](https://github.com/tidyverse/nycflights13)
package: one reading an hour at Newark, JFK and LaGuardia for the whole year,
26,000 rows, taken from NOAA's Integrated Surface Database.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
w <- as.data.frame(nycflights13::weather)
w <- w[!is.na(w$temp), ]
# One known bad reading: 13 °F at JFK on a May evening.
w <- w[!(w$origin == "JFK" &
         w$time_hour == as.POSIXct("2013-05-08 22:00", tz = "America/New_York")), ]

w$temp_c <- (w$temp - 32) * 5 / 9
# Weeks of seven days from 1 January; the last day of the year joins week 52.
w$week <- pmin((as.integer(format(w$time_hour, "%j")) - 1) %/% 7 + 1, 52)
# The first level sits at the bottom, so put week 52 first: January on top.
w$week <- factor(w$week, levels = 52:1)
w$airport <- c(EWR = "Newark", JFK = "JFK", LGA = "LaGuardia")[w$origin]
```
:::


## What is drawn

`mark_ridgeline()` takes a numeric `x` and a categorical `y`, estimates a kernel
density of `x` for each level of `y`, and draws it as a filled outline sitting on
that row. `height` sets how tall a ridge may grow in units of the row spacing:
the default of 1.4 lets neighbours overlap a little, and 4 here lets the summer
peaks climb well into the rows above.

The look comes from two settings. Every ridge is filled black, the colour of the
page, and stroked in off-white. Each ridge is drawn after the one above it, so
its fill covers whatever it overlaps, and the lines behind disappear where they
should. `theme_void()` drops the axes, gridlines and panel, and one
`axis.text.x` element puts back the temperature scale along the bottom.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ink <- "#f4eee0"

p <- vplot(w, width = 6, height = 7.5) |>
  mark_ridgeline(x = temp_c, y = week, height = 4, linewidth = 0.5,
                 fill = "black", color = "#f4eee0") |>
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(-10, 0, 10, 20, 30),
                     labels = c("−10 °C", "0 °C", "10 °C", "20 °C", "30 °C")) |>
  labs(
    title = "FIFTY-TWO WEEKS OF NEW YORK",
    subtitle = "Hourly air temperature at Newark, JFK and LaGuardia in 2013,\none ridge per week, January at the top",
    caption = "Data: nycflights13::weather (NOAA Integrated Surface Database)"
  ) |>
  theme_void() |>
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "black", color = NA),
    plot.title = element_text(color = ink, size = 20, hjust = 0.5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "#a8a294", size = 10, hjust = 0.5),
    plot.caption = element_text(color = "#6f6a60", size = 8),
    axis.text.x = element_text(color = "#a8a294", size = 9)
  )
```
:::


The stroke colour is written out as a string, not as `ink`. A mark argument that
names a variable is read as a mapping, the way `color = species` is, so
`color = ink` would put a one-entry legend on the poster. The theme elements
take ordinary values, so `ink` works there.


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](figs/ridgeline-poster.png){fig-alt='Fifty-two white density ridges on black, one per week of 2013, stacked top to bottom: narrow cold ridges at the top, wide warm ones shifted right in the middle, cold ones again at the bottom' width=100%}
:::
:::


Read it top to bottom and the year goes by. January's ridges are low and wide,
spread across twenty degrees by cold snaps and thaws. Through the spring they
drift right and grow taller, and by July a week's temperatures sit in a tight
band near 25–30 °C. In the last weeks the ridges spread out and move back left.
Weeks with two peaks are weeks where the weather changed: a cold front halfway
through splits the readings in two.

## Three airports

The three airports are a few kilometres apart, but not the same place. JFK sits
on Jamaica Bay, LaGuardia on the East River, Newark inland across the Hudson.
`transition_states(airport)` draws the poster once per airport and morphs each
week's ridge from one outline to the next. The scales are trained once over all
three, so the ridges move against a fixed axis.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
a <- p |>
  labs(subtitle = "Hourly air temperature at {closest_state} in 2013,\none ridge per week, January at the top") |>
  transition_states(airport) |>
  animate(nframes = 45, fps = 15)
```
:::



::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](figs/ridgeline-airports.gif){fig-alt='Animation of the ridgeline poster morphing between Newark, JFK and LaGuardia; the summer ridges shift slightly between airports' width=100%}
:::
:::


The differences are small and they are in summer. At Newark and LaGuardia the
June-to-August ridges reach a degree or two further right than at JFK, where
the sea breeze off the bay keeps the hottest afternoons cooler (the 95th
percentile of summer readings is 32 °C at the first two, 30 °C at JFK). The winter weeks barely move. The poster is two colours, so
this one is saved as a GIF: it needs nothing beyond GIF's 256 colours, and comes
out at half the size of an animated PNG.
